exploration.title: Pattern Palace
exploration.subject: Mathematics
exploration.summary: Compare a quarter-turn with a reflection, then calculate how regular-polygon corners fit around one point.
exploration.question: What changes when a motif is turned or reflected, and when does a regular-polygon corner total fill 360°?
exploration.explanation: A rotation turns every point through the same angle around a center. A reflection maps points across a line. Both are rigid transformations, so corresponding lengths and angles stay equal, but a reflection reverses orientation while a rotation does not. Around one point, regular-polygon interior angles must total 360° to meet without a local gap or overlap. This corner calculation is evidence about that point; one finite arrangement alone is not proof that a proposed rule continues across the whole plane.

experiments.title: Turn or flip?
experiments.instruction: Keep the asymmetric motif, center and marked point M fixed. Predict whether a 90° clockwise turn or a reflection across the vertical line moves M farther right, then compare both images.
experiments.observe: The turn puts M 18 units right and 30 units up; the reflection puts M 30 units right and 18 units up. Explain how the positions differ even though corresponding lengths and angles stay equal.

experiments.title: Fill a full turn
experiments.instruction: Keep the regular-pentagon shape, side length, 108° interior angle and meeting point fixed. Three corners leave 36°. Predict what happens when a fourth pentagon is added, then compare both totals.
experiments.observe: Three corners total 324° and leave 36°; four total 432° and overlap by 72°. Explain why adding a whole 108° corner cannot fill only the 36° gap.

exploration.misconception: Seeing a 360° fit at one corner is not by itself proof that a proposed pattern tiles the plane. The arrangement must continue consistently at every point, and regular and irregular polygons with the same number of sides are not interchangeable.
